summary.text: For an arbitrary bound \(b\), apply the hypothesis to \(n=(6(b+1)+1)!/6\), obtaining a Sophie Germain prime \(p=6x-1\) and a twin pair \(q-2,q\), where \(q=6y+1\) and \((6(b+1)+1)!=p+q\). If \(p\) or \(q-2\) were at most \(6(b+1)\), factorial divisibility would make one of the primes divide the other, forcing equality, contrary to \(p\equiv-1\pmod 6\) and \(q\equiv1\pmod 6\); thus both families are unbounded and hence infinite.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
S=\{p\in\mathbb N:p\text{ is prime and }2p+1\text{ is prime}\}
\]
be the set of Sophie Germain primes, and let
\[
T=\{p\in\mathbb N:p\text{ is prime and }p+2\text{ is prime}\}
\]
be the set of lower members of twin-prime pairs.

For a positive integer \(n\), the number \(A227923(n)\) is the sum, over integers \(x\) with \(1\le x<n\), of the indicator of the following four simultaneous primality conditions:
\[
6x-1\text{ is prime},\qquad 12x-1\text{ is prime},
\]
\[
6(n-x)-1\text{ is prime},\qquad 6(n-x)+1\text{ is prime}.
\]
Thus the first two conditions say that \(6x-1\) is a Sophie Germain prime, since
\[
2(6x-1)+1=12x-1,
\]
and the last two say that \(6(n-x)-1\) and \(6(n-x)+1\) form a twin-prime pair.

Assume throughout that
\[
A227923(n)>0\qquad\text{for every integer }n>1.
\]
We prove that both \(S\) and \(T\) are infinite.

First note the immediate witness-extraction consequence of the hypothesis. Since \(A227923(n)\) is a finite sum of terms each equal to either \(0\) or \(1\), if \(A227923(n)>0\), then at least one summand is \(1\). Consequently, for every \(n>1\), there is an integer \(x\) such that
\[
1\le x<n
\]
and all four numbers
\[
6x-1,\quad 12x-1,\quad 6(n-x)-1,\quad 6(n-x)+1
\]
are prime. If we put
\[
y=n-x,
\]
then \(y\ge1\), \(x+y=n\), and the four primes are
\[
6x-1,\quad 12x-1,\quad 6y-1,\quad 6y+1.
\]

We next give the factorial construction that will be used for both infinitude claims. Let \(N\) be any nonnegative integer and define
\[
M=6(N+1),\qquad n=\frac{(M+1)!}{6}.
\]
This is an integer: indeed \(M+1\ge7\), and hence \(3!=6\) divides \((M+1)!\). Moreover,
\[
6n=(M+1)!.
\]
Also \((M+1)!\ge7!=5040\), so \(n\ge840>1\). We may therefore apply the assumed positivity to this \(n\). It yields positive integers \(x,y\), with \(x+y=n\), for which
\[
P:=6x-1,
\qquad 2P+1=12x-1,
\qquad R:=6y-1,
\qquad Q:=6y+1
\]
are all prime. The crucial identity is
\[
(M+1)!=6n=6(x+y)=(6x-1)+(6y+1)=P+Q. \tag{1}
\]

We first prove that the twin-prime set \(T\) is infinite. It is enough to show that it has no upper bound, because every finite set of natural numbers has an upper bound.

Suppose, to the contrary, that \(T\) has an upper bound \(b\); thus every lower member of a twin-prime pair is at most \(b\). Apply the preceding factorial construction with \(N=b\). Then
\[
M=6(b+1),
\]
and we obtain positive \(x,y\) and primes \(P=6x-1\), \(Q=6y+1\), and \(R=6y-1\), satisfying (1). We claim that
\[
R=6y-1>M. \tag{2}
\]

Assume instead that \(6y-1\le M\). Since both \(6y\) and \(M\) are divisible by \(6\), this implies \(6y\le M\), and hence
\[
Q=6y+1\le M+1.
\]
Also \(Q\ge7\), because \(y\ge1\). Therefore \(Q\) is one of the positive integers not exceeding \(M+1\), so
\[
Q\mid (M+1)!.
\]
By (1), \((M+1)!=P+Q\). Since \(Q\) divides both \((M+1)!\) and \(Q\), it follows that \(Q\mid P\).

But \(P\) is prime. Every positive divisor of a prime is either \(1\) or the prime itself. The possibility \(Q=1\) is excluded by \(Q\ge7\), so we would have \(Q=P\). This is impossible: \(Q=6y+1\) is congruent to \(1\pmod 6\), while \(P=6x-1\) is congruent to \(5\pmod 6\). Equivalently, their equality would give \(6(x-y)=2\), which has no integer solutions. This contradiction proves (2).

Now \(R=6y-1\) belongs to \(T\), because both \(R\) and
\[
R+2=6y+1=Q
\]
are prime. On the other hand, (2) and \(M=6(b+1)\) give
\[
R>M=6(b+1)>b,
\]
contradicting the assumption that \(b\) bounds \(T\). Thus \(T\) is unbounded and therefore infinite. In particular, there are infinitely many twin-prime pairs.

We now prove that the Sophie Germain prime set \(S\) is infinite. Again, it suffices to prove that it has no upper bound.

Suppose, to the contrary, that every element of \(S\) is at most some natural number \(b\). Apply the same construction with \(N=b\), so that
\[
M=6(b+1),
\]
and obtain positive \(x,y\) and the primes
\[
P=6x-1,
\qquad 12x-1,
\qquad 6y-1,
\qquad Q=6y+1,
\]
with \((M+1)!=P+Q\). We claim that
\[
P=6x-1>M. \tag{3}
\]

Suppose instead that \(P\le M\). Then certainly \(P\le M+1\). Since \(P\) is positive, it follows that
\[
P\mid (M+1)!.
\]
Using again the identity
\[
(M+1)!=P+Q,
\]
we find that \(P\mid Q\). Since \(Q\) is prime, a positive divisor of \(Q\) must be either \(1\) or \(Q\). The first possibility cannot occur because \(P=6x-1\ge5\) as \(x\ge1\). Thus \(P=Q\). As before, this is impossible because
\[
P\equiv5\pmod6,
\qquad Q\equiv1\pmod6.
\]
This proves (3).

Finally, \(P\) belongs to \(S\): it is prime by construction, and
\[
2P+1=2(6x-1)+1=12x-1
\]
is also prime. But (3) gives
\[
P>M=6(b+1)>b,
\]
contradicting the assumption that \(b\) is an upper bound for \(S\). Hence \(S\) is unbounded and therefore infinite.

We have shown that the assumed positivity of \(A227923(n)\) for every \(n>1\) forces both the set of Sophie Germain primes and the set of lower members of twin-prime pairs to be infinite. Therefore there are infinitely many Sophie Germain primes and infinitely many twin-prime pairs.
